course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: The Global Tapestry
unit.description: Explore how societies organized power, shared beliefs, and built their economies across the world.

themes.title: Interactions of humans with the environment
themes.question: How did geography, crops, resources, or disease shape choices?
themes.example: Andean terraces made steep slopes more usable for farming.

themes.title: Social interactions and organization
themes.question: Who had status, opportunities, or obligations?
themes.example: Examination preparation favored families that could afford education.

themes.title: Political systems and governance
themes.question: How did rulers gain authority and administer territory?
themes.example: Song officials carried imperial decisions into local government.

themes.title: Economic systems
themes.question: How were goods produced, exchanged, taxed, or distributed?
themes.example: Mali drew revenue from commerce through its territory.

themes.title: Cultural developments and interactions
themes.question: How did beliefs, learning, and artistic practices influence society?
themes.example: Buddhist monasteries connected religious practice with education.

themes.title: Technology and innovation
themes.question: What techniques or tools changed what people could do?
themes.example: Inca roads and knotted records helped officials coordinate resources.

questions.prompt: Which comparison of Mali and the Hausa city-states is accurate?
choices: Mali built a large empire, while Hausa cities were provinces within it
Both were ruled by a single dynasty that united West Africa after 1250
Mali built a large empire, while Hausa cities kept separate rulers
Both were coastal states that depended mainly on Indian Ocean trade
questions.explanation: Mali expanded into an empire under one ruler, while Hausa city-states such as Kano governed themselves.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.5 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Mali's empire is right, but the Hausa cities were independent, not Malian provinces.
No single dynasty united West Africa; Mali and the Hausa cities were separate.
Mali expanded into an empire under one ruler, while Hausa city-states such as Kano governed themselves.
Both were inland states linked to Saharan and regional trade.
questions.distinguisher: Compare the scale of political authority.

questions.prompt: How did trans-Saharan exchange contribute to Mali’s political power?
choices: Revenue from trade helped rulers support armies and administration
Gold exports gave Mali's rulers control over North African states
Caravan merchants elected Mali's rulers and paid them salaries
Revenue from trade replaced farming as the main way most people lived
questions.explanation: Taxes and control of routes gave rulers wealth to fund soldiers and officials.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.5 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Taxes and control of routes gave rulers wealth to fund soldiers and officials.
Mali traded with North Africa but did not rule it.
Mali's rulers came from a royal lineage; merchants did not choose them.
Trade enriched rulers, but most people in Mali still farmed or herded.
questions.distinguisher: Trade funded the state; it did not replace the economy's base.

questions.prompt: How could Mansa Musa’s pilgrimage support his authority?
choices: It allowed him to claim the throne of Egypt during his stay in Cairo
It showed his wealth and led every Malian subject to convert to Islam
It won him a title from the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad that ended local rivalries
It showed his wealth and tied him to influential Muslim scholars and rulers
questions.explanation: The pilgrimage advertised Mali's riches and strengthened ties with the Islamic world.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.5 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Musa visited Cairo as a pilgrim, not as a claimant to Egypt's throne.
Wealth is right, but many subjects kept local religious practices.
The Abbasid caliphate in Baghdad had ended in 1258, decades before the pilgrimage.
The pilgrimage advertised Mali's riches and strengthened ties with the Islamic world.
questions.distinguisher: Visibility and connection, not mass conversion or conquest.

questions.prompt: Which interpretation of Swahili cities best accounts for African and imported cultural elements?
choices: African communities built the cities, but Arab settlers governed them all
African communities shaped cities that were linked to overseas trade
Arab and Persian settlers founded the cities, and Africans only traded there
The cities copied Arabian culture completely, including its main language
questions.explanation: Swahili cities were African urban societies that absorbed influences through trade.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.5 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: African builders are right, but the cities had their own rulers, often of local origin.
Swahili cities were African urban societies that absorbed influences through trade.
The older claim that outsiders founded these cities is not supported by evidence.
Swahili is a Bantu language; Arabic contributed vocabulary, not replacement.
questions.distinguisher: Connection does not mean foreign control.

questions.prompt: What would imported ceramics found at Great Zimbabwe most directly suggest?
choices: The city's builders learned stone construction from Chinese workers
The inland city was linked to distant trade through coastal networks
The city's people depended on imported food from the coast
The inland city was ruled by foreign merchants who brought the ceramics
questions.explanation: Imported goods show connections reaching the city through Swahili and Indian Ocean trade.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.5 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: The dry-stone building tradition was local.
Imported goods show connections reaching the city through Swahili and Indian Ocean trade.
Ceramics show trade connections, not food dependence; farming and cattle supported the city.
Imports show contact, not foreign rule; Shona ancestors built and governed the site.

questions.prompt: How do Lalibela’s churches challenge the claim that African state building relied exclusively on Islam?
choices: They show that Ethiopia was cut off from other regions
They show Christian patronage, so Islam played no role in Africa
They show that Ethiopia was ruled from Rome by the pope
They show Christian patronage connected to Ethiopian kingship
questions.explanation: Rock-hewn churches built with royal support show a Christian state with its own institutions.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.5 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Ethiopia traded with and fought Muslim neighbors and kept ties to Egypt.
Christian patronage disproves the exclusive claim, but Islam remained important elsewhere in Africa.
Ethiopian Christianity was linked to the Coptic Church in Egypt, not Rome.
Rock-hewn churches built with royal support show a Christian state with its own institutions.
questions.distinguisher: A counterexample disproves an “exclusively” claim without replacing it with another extreme.

questions.prompt: Why should a historian examine the context of a griot’s account?
choices: Its audience and transmission can shape how rulers and events are remembered
Its audience shaped it, so oral accounts cannot be used as historical evidence
Griots recorded events in writing at the moment they happened
Griots were foreign visitors who did not understand local traditions
questions.explanation: Griots often performed for patrons and passed accounts down over generations, which shapes what is preserved.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.5 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Griots often performed for patrons and passed accounts down over generations, which shapes what is preserved.
Context matters, but oral tradition is valuable evidence when weighed carefully.
Griots preserved history orally, often long after events.
Griots were members of West African societies and keepers of local tradition.
questions.distinguisher: Sourcing applies to oral sources just as it does to written ones.

questions.prompt: What is a problem with saying kin-based societies had no government?
choices: It ignores that these societies wrote down detailed law codes
It ignores that these societies had no conflicts to resolve
It ignores institutions that organized decisions and settled disputes
It ignores that these societies were all ruled by Mali's emperors
questions.explanation: Elders, lineage heads, and chiefs governed land, labor, and disputes without a central state.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.5 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Many such societies governed through oral custom rather than written codes.
All societies have conflicts; the point is that they had ways to resolve them.
Elders, lineage heads, and chiefs governed land, labor, and disputes without a central state.
Many kin-based communities lay outside Mali's control.
questions.distinguisher: No central king is not the same as no government.

choices: Silk Roads caravans

Mediterranean galleys

questions.prompt: Which of the following conclusions about Abash is best supported by the passage?
choices: It was isolated from contact with other states and religions
It was a Christian state ruled directly by the Byzantine emperor
It was a Christian state whose ruler had authority over other kings
It was a Muslim sultanate allied with the ruler of Aden
questions.explanation: Polo says the greatest of the six kings is a Christian to whom the others are subject.
choiceExplanations: The passage mentions wars with neighbors and a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, evidence of contact.
Polo describes a Christian king of Abash, not Byzantine rule.
Polo says the greatest of the six kings is a Christian to whom the others are subject.
Polo describes Abash as at war with the Soldan of Aden.
questions.distinguisher: Ethiopia was Christian, but it had its own kings; Polo says the greatest of its six kings was its overlord.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Marco Polo, Venetian merchant who traveled in Mongol-ruled Asia c. 1271–1295, account dictated to the writer Rustichello of Pisa, c. 1298, describing the Christian kingdom of Ethiopia from reports he heard in Indian Ocean ports
stimulusBlocks.citation: The Book of Ser Marco Polo, trans. Henry Yule, rev. Henri Cordier, 3rd ed. (London: John Murray, 1903), vol. 2, Book III, ch. 35. Project Gutenberg eBook #12410.
stimulusBlocks.note: Abash is Abyssinia (Ethiopia); Polo, like many Europeans, called distant lands a part of “India.” Saracens means Muslims. Aden is a port in Yemen. Polo did not visit Ethiopia.
stimulusBlocks.text:
Abash is a very great Province, and you must know that it constitutes the MIDDLE INDIA; and it is on the mainland. There are in it six great Kings with six great Kingdoms; and of these six Kings there are three that are Christians and three that are Saracens; but the greatest of all the six is a Christian, and all the others are subject to him. . . .

The people here are excellent soldiers, and they go on horseback, for they have horses in plenty. Well they may; for they are in daily war with the Soldan of ADEN, and with the Nubians, and a variety of other nations. . . .

You must know that this Christian King, who is the Lord of the Province of Abash, declared his intention to go on pilgrimage to Jerusalem to adore the Holy Sepulchre of Our Lord God Jesus Christ the Saviour. But his Barons said that for him to go in person would be to run too great a risk; and they recommended him to send some bishop or prelate in his stead.

questions.prompt: The Christian kingship described in the passage is best understood in the context of
choices: a Christian tradition in the region dating back to the kingdom of Aksum
a Christian tradition introduced to the region by crusaders from Europe
Mongol conquests that spread Christianity in Northeast Africa
the recent arrival of Portuguese missionaries on the East African coast
questions.explanation: Ethiopian Christianity grew out of Aksum's conversion in the fourth century, and the Solomonic dynasty claimed that heritage.
choiceExplanations: Ethiopian Christianity grew out of Aksum's conversion in the fourth century, and the Solomonic dynasty claimed that heritage.
Ethiopian Christianity was much older than the Crusades.
The Mongols did not conquer Northeast Africa.
Portuguese missionaries arrived after 1500, too late for Polo's account.
questions.distinguisher: There was a long Christian tradition, but it came from Aksum's conversion centuries earlier, not from crusaders.

questions.prompt: Which of the following most limits the usefulness of the passage as evidence about Ethiopia?
choices: Polo wrote it in Arabic for a Muslim audience in Aden
Polo based it on Ethiopian royal chronicles that he translated
Polo wrote it while serving as an official of the Ethiopian king
Polo based it on reports he heard rather than on his own observation

choiceExplanations: Polo's book was written for European readers, not in Arabic.

questions.prompt: The Chinese porcelain and Persian pottery found at Great Zimbabwe are best used as evidence that
choices: Great Zimbabwe was built by merchants from China and Persia
Great Zimbabwe was connected to Indian Ocean trade networks
Great Zimbabwe was connected to trans-Saharan trade routes
Great Zimbabwe produced porcelain for export
questions.explanation: Goods from China and Persia reached the site through the Swahili coast and Indian Ocean trade.
choiceExplanations: Imported goods show connection, not foreign builders; the passage rejects that claim.
Goods from China and Persia reached the site through the Swahili coast and Indian Ocean trade.
Great Zimbabwe traded toward the east coast, not across the Sahara.
The porcelain was imported, not made at the site.
questions.distinguisher: Long-distance connection is right, but Great Zimbabwe's goods moved toward the Swahili coast and the Indian Ocean, not across the Sahara.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 1.5, KC-3.2.I.D.ii: in Africa, state systems demonstrated continuity, innovation, and diversity; Great Zimbabwe is an illustrative example
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing archaeological evidence about Great Zimbabwe, c. 1200–1450
stimulusBlocks.text:
Great Zimbabwe, built by ancestors of the Shona people, was the capital of a state in southern Africa between about 1200 and 1450. Its stone enclosures were built without mortar, and the largest wall is more than 9 meters high in places. Cattle herding and farming supported the population, while rulers controlled trade in gold and ivory that moved toward the Swahili coast.

Archaeologists have found Chinese porcelain, Persian pottery, and glass beads at the site. In the 1800s, some European writers claimed that Africans could not have built the walls. Archaeological research has shown that claim to be false.

questions.prompt: The claims made by some European writers in the 1800s, described in the passage, were most likely shaped by
choices: the oral traditions of Shona-speaking communities
racist assumptions used to justify European colonial expansion
careful study of Arabic accounts written by visiting merchants
careful archaeological excavation of the stone enclosures
questions.explanation: Denying African achievement supported racist ideas used to justify colonial rule in the 1800s.
choiceExplanations: Shona traditions connected the site to their own ancestors, contradicting the writers' claim.
Denying African achievement supported racist ideas used to justify colonial rule in the 1800s.
No such accounts support the writers' claim; it rested on assumptions, not evidence.
Archaeological research disproved the claim.
questions.distinguisher: Shona oral traditions linked the site to African ancestors; they would not support the claim that Africans could not build it.

questions.prompt: Which aspect of Mali's government does Ibn Battuta praise most directly in the passage?
choices: Its policy of forcing all subjects to convert to Islam
Its success in keeping order by confiscating foreign property
Its system of examinations for selecting officials
Its success in keeping order and protecting travelers
questions.explanation: He stresses security: neither travelers nor residents feared robbers.
choiceExplanations: He praises Muslim devotion but does not describe forced conversion.
He says the property of a foreigner who dies is kept safe for the rightful heir.
Mali did not use civil service examinations.
He stresses security: neither travelers nor residents feared robbers.
questions.distinguisher: Order is right, but Ibn Battuta says Mali did not confiscate the property of foreigners who died there.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Ibn Battuta, Muslim legal scholar from Morocco who traveled c. 1325–1354, account dictated to the writer Ibn Juzayy, 1355, describing his stay in the Mali Empire, 1352–1353
stimulusBlocks.citation: Ibn Battuta, Travels in Asia and Africa, 1325–1354, trans. H. A. R. Gibb (London: George Routledge & Sons, 1929), ch. 14. Checked against Internet Archive scan travelsinasiaafr0000ibnb, scan pp. 351–352.
stimulusBlocks.note: Bracketed words replace the translator's dated term for West Africans. “White men” refers to North African and Arab visitors and merchants.
stimulusBlocks.text:
[The people of Mali] possess some admirable qualities. They are seldom unjust, and have a greater abhorrence of injustice than any other people. Their sultan shows no mercy to anyone who is guilty of the least act of it. There is complete security in their country. Neither traveller nor inhabitant in it has anything to fear from robbers or men of violence. They do not confiscate the property of any white man who dies in their country, even if it be uncounted wealth. On the contrary, they give it into the charge of some trustworthy person among the whites, until the rightful heir takes possession of it. They are careful to observe the hours of prayer, and assiduous in attending them in congregations, and in bringing up their children to them. . . .

Yet another is their zeal for learning the Koran by heart. . . . Among their bad qualities are the following. . . . Then there is their custom of putting dust and ashes on their heads, as a mark of respect, and the grotesque ceremonies we have described when the poets recite their verses.

questions.prompt: Ibn Battuta's observations of Islamic practice in Mali are best explained by
choices: the spread of Islam through trans-Saharan trade and the patronage of Mali's rulers
the conquest of Mali by Mamluk armies from Egypt
the spread of Islam through trans-Saharan trade, which quickly ended all local traditions
the work of Christian missionaries who taught Arabic in Timbuktu
questions.explanation: Muslim merchants and rulers such as Mansa Musa supported mosques and learning in Mali.
choiceExplanations: Muslim merchants and rulers such as Mansa Musa supported mosques and learning in Mali.
Mali was never conquered by the Mamluks.
Ibn Battuta criticizes customs such as dust on heads, which shows local traditions continued.
Islamic learning in Timbuktu was supported by Muslim scholars, not Christian missionaries.
questions.distinguisher: Trade did spread Islam, but Ibn Battuta's own complaints show local customs continued.
